agent_reasoning: Merged diff composed mechanically by cherry-picking fix 041a6c36142f on top of intro b8bf2f4e1758 via git's 3-way merge. Vulnerability (NullPointerDereference): In common_init(), when parsing channel layouts from the deprecated 'ch_layouts' option string, av_realloc_array() is called to grow buf->channel_layouts. The return value is stored in the local variable 'tmp', but is never assigned back to buf->channel_layouts. Since av_realloc_array() may free the original buffer and return a pointer to a newly allocated buffer (or return a new allocation when the original pointer is NULL), buf->channel_layouts remains stale (NULL on the first iteration, or a dangling pointer on subsequent iterations). The immediately following memset() on line 208 dereferences buf->channel_layouts, causing a null pointer dereference crash (SEGV). Additionally, the memset only zeroes sizeof(*buf->channel_layouts) bytes (one element) instead of sizeof(*buf->channel_layouts) * 2 bytes (the new element plus the terminator), leaving the terminator element uninitialized. This is triggered by filter graphs containing abuffersink with channel layout options, e.g. 'abuffersink=::a'. Root cause: After calling av_realloc_array() to grow the channel_layouts array, the new pointer stored in 'tmp' was never assigned back to buf->channel_layouts. This is a classic realloc pattern bug where the caller forgets to update the original pointer. On the first iteration, buf->channel_layouts is NULL, so the memset writes to address 0x0. On subsequent iterations, if realloc moved the buffer, buf->channel_layouts becomes a dangling pointer (use-after-free). A secondary issue is that the memset only clears one element instead of two (the new entry plus the zero terminator).

Vulnerability (LogicError): In audio_element_obu(), the num_parameters value is read from untrusted input via ffio_read_leb() without an upper bound check when audio_element_type is 0 (Channel representations). A crafted IAMF file can supply num_parameters > 2, causing the subsequent loop to call param_parse() with duplicate parameter types. agent_reasoning: Merged diff composed mechanically by cherry-picking fix 35ea45835484 on top of intro f8d429e0c569 via git's 3-way merge. Vulnerability (BufferOverflow): In filter_frame(), the index j is computed as s->fft_len - s->remaining_fill (later changed to s->fft_len/2 + s->remaining_fill_max - s->remaining_fill by a subsequent commit). After processing a CQT frame, s->remaining_fill is set to step, where step = sample_rate / (fps * count). When timeclamp and/or fps are low, fft_len can be small relative to step (e.g., timeclamp=0.01 at 44100Hz gives fft_len=512, while fps=15 count=5 gives step=588). This makes j negative (512 - 588 = -76). The subsequent loops iterate starting at m=0, writing to s->fft_data[j+m] with negative indices, causing heap buffer overflow (writes before the allocated buffer). This corrupts heap metadata, leading to SIGSEGV crashes, double-free errors, malloc assertion failures, and corrupted double-linked list errors depending on what memory is overwritten. The rewrite commit introduced this by changing fps from a bounded integer (10-100) to AV_OPT_TYPE_VIDEO_RATE with no practical lower bound, and removing the rate%(fps*count)==0 divisibility check, allowing step to exceed fft_len. Root cause: The rewrite of showcqt in commit f8d429e0c56 relaxed the fps parameter from a bounded integer (10-100) to an unbounded VIDEO_RATE type and removed the divisibility check (rate % (fps*count) == 0). This allowed configurations where the step size (sample_rate / (fps * count)) exceeds fft_len (2^ceil(log2(sample_rate * timeclamp))). After the first CQT plot, remaining_fill is set to step, and on the next loop iteration j = fft_len - remaining_fill becomes negative. The loop starting at m=0 then writes to fft_data at negative offsets, corrupting the heap. A subsequent commit (c4a3526b57d) further lowered the timeclamp minimum from 0.1 to 0.002, making the bug much easier to trigger with moderate fps values.

[Merged] avfilter/avf_showcqt: rewrite showcqt and add features

add yuv444p, yuv422p, and yuv420p output format (lower cpu usage
on ffplay playback because it does not do format conversion)
custom size with size/s option (fullhd option is deprecated)
custom layout with bar_h, axis_h, and sono_h option
support rational frame rate (within fps/r/rate option)
relaxed frame rate restriction (support fractional sample step)
support all input sample rates
separate sonogram and bargraph volume (with volume/sono_v and
volume2/bar_v)
timeclamp option alias (timeclamp/tc)
fcount option
gamma option alias (gamma/sono_g and gamma2/bar_g)
support custom frequency range (basefreq and endfreq)
support drawing axis using external image file (axisfile option)
alias for disabling drawing to axis (text/axis)
possibility to optimize it using arch specific asm code

+static void cqt_calc(FFTComplex *dst, const FFTComplex *src, const Coeffs *coeffs,
+                     int len, int fft_len)
+{
+    int k, x, i, j;
+    for (k = 0; k < len; k++) {
+        FFTComplex l, r, a = {0,0}, b = {0,0};
+
+        for (x = 0; x < coeffs[k].len; x++) {
+            FFTSample u = coeffs[k].val[x];
+            i = coeffs[k].start + x;
+            j = fft_len - i;
+            a.re += u * src[i].re;
+            a.im += u * src[i].im;
+            b.re += u * src[j].re;
+            b.im += u * src[j].im;
+        }
+
+        /* separate left and right, (and multiply by 2.0) */
+        l.re = a.re + b.re;
+        l.im = a.im - b.im;
+        r.re = b.im + a.im;
+        r.im = b.re - a.re;
+        dst[k].re = l.re * l.re + l.im * l.im;
+        dst[k].im = r.re * r.re + r.im * r.im;
+    }
+}

+{

+        end = fmin(s->fft_len, floor(center + 0.5 * flen));

+        nb_cqt_coeffs += s->coeffs[m].len;

+    out->height = h;

+        av_frame_free(&out);
+        return NULL;
+    }
+    if (format == AV_PIX_FMT_RGB24 || format == AV_PIX_FMT_RGBA) {
+        memset(out->data[0], 0, out->linesize[0] * h);
+    } else {
+        int hh = (format == AV_PIX_FMT_YUV420P || format == AV_PIX_FMT_YUVA420P) ? h / 2 : h;
+        memset(out->data[0], 16, out->linesize[0] * h);
+        memset(out->data[1], 128, out->linesize[1] * hh);
+        memset(out->data[2], 128, out->linesize[2] * hh);
+        if (out->data[3])
+            memset(out->data[3], 0, out->linesize[3] * h);
+    }

intro_commit_message:
avfilter/avf_showcqt: rewrite showcqt and add features

add yuv444p, yuv422p, and yuv420p output format (lower cpu usage
on ffplay playback because it does not do format conversion)
custom size with size/s option (fullhd option is deprecated)
custom layout with bar_h, axis_h, and sono_h option
support rational frame rate (within fps/r/rate option)
relaxed frame rate restriction (support fractional sample step)
support all input sample rates
separate sonogram and bargraph volume (with volume/sono_v and
volume2/bar_v)
timeclamp option alias (timeclamp/tc)
fcount option
gamma option alias (gamma/sono_g and gamma2/bar_g)
support custom frequency range (basefreq and endfreq)
support drawing axis using external image file (axisfile option)
alias for disabling drawing to axis (text/axis)
possibility to optimize it using arch specific asm code

Signed-off-by: Michael Niedermayer <michael@niedermayer.cc>

+static void cqt_calc(FFTComplex *dst, const FFTComplex *src, const Coeffs *coeffs,
+                     int len, int fft_len)
+{
+    int k, x, i, j;
+    for (k = 0; k < len; k++) {
+        FFTComplex l, r, a = {0,0}, b = {0,0};
+
+        for (x = 0; x < coeffs[k].len; x++) {
+            FFTSample u = coeffs[k].val[x];
+            i = coeffs[k].start + x;
+            j = fft_len - i;
+            a.re += u * src[i].re;
+            a.im += u * src[i].im;
+            b.re += u * src[j].re;
+            b.im += u * src[j].im;
+        }
+
+        /* separate left and right, (and multiply by 2.0) */
+        l.re = a.re + b.re;
+        l.im = a.im - b.im;
+        r.re = b.im + a.im;
+        r.im = b.re - a.re;
+        dst[k].re = l.re * l.re + l.im * l.im;
+        dst[k].im = r.re * r.re + r.im * r.im;
+    }
+}

+{

+        end = fmin(s->fft_len, floor(center + 0.5 * flen));

+        nb_cqt_coeffs += s->coeffs[m].len;

+    out->height = h;

+        av_frame_free(&out);
+        return NULL;
+    }
+    if (format == AV_PIX_FMT_RGB24 || format == AV_PIX_FMT_RGBA) {
+        memset(out->data[0], 0, out->linesize[0] * h);
+    } else {
+        int hh = (format == AV_PIX_FMT_YUV420P || format == AV_PIX_FMT_YUVA420P) ? h / 2 : h;
+        memset(out->data[0], 16, out->linesize[0] * h);
+        memset(out->data[1], 128, out->linesize[1] * hh);
+        memset(out->data[2], 128, out->linesize[2] * hh);
+        if (out->data[3])
+            memset(out->data[3], 0, out->linesize[3] * h);
+    }

findings.message: In filter_frame(), the index j is computed as s->fft_len - s->remaining_fill (later changed to s->fft_len/2 + s->remaining_fill_max - s->remaining_fill by a subsequent commit). After processing a CQT frame, s->remaining_fill is set to step, where step = sample_rate / (fps * count). When timeclamp and/or fps are low, fft_len can be small relative to step (e.g., timeclamp=0.01 at 44100Hz gives fft_len=512, while fps=15 count=5 gives step=588). This makes j negative (512 - 588 = -76). The subsequent loops iterate starting at m=0, writing to s->fft_data[j+m] with negative indices, causing heap buffer overflow (writes before the allocated buffer). This corrupts heap metadata, leading to SIGSEGV crashes, double-free errors, malloc assertion failures, and corrupted double-linked list errors depending on what memory is overwritten. The rewrite commit introduced this by changing fps from a bounded integer (10-100) to AV_OPT_TYPE_VIDEO_RATE with no practical lower bound, and removing the rate%(fps*count)==0 divisibility check, allowing step to exceed fft_len.
findings.suggestion: Clamp the loop start index to ensure j+m is never negative. Replace 'for (m = 0; ...' with 'for (m = FFMAX(0, -j); ...' in both loops that write to s->fft_data[j+m].

ground_truth.root_cause: The rewrite of showcqt in commit f8d429e0c56 relaxed the fps parameter from a bounded integer (10-100) to an unbounded VIDEO_RATE type and removed the divisibility check (rate % (fps*count) == 0). This allowed configurations where the step size (sample_rate / (fps * count)) exceeds fft_len (2^ceil(log2(sample_rate * timeclamp))). After the first CQT plot, remaining_fill is set to step, and on the next loop iteration j = fft_len - remaining_fill becomes negative. The loop starting at m=0 then writes to fft_data at negative offsets, corrupting the heap. A subsequent commit (c4a3526b57d) further lowered the timeclamp minimum from 0.1 to 0.002, making the bug much easier to trigger with moderate fps values.

agent_reasoning: Merged diff composed mechanically by cherry-picking fix 45daaf2caaa3 on top of intro 6e225123d858 via git's 3-way merge. Vulnerability (LogicError): The refactoring in commit 6e225123d replaced a byte-by-byte `put_bits` loop with a single `ff_copy_bits()` call. However, `ff_copy_bits()` expects its third argument `length` to be the number of **bits** to copy (as documented in put_bits.h: '@param length the number of bits of src to copy'). The code passes `side_data->size`, which is a byte count. This means only `side_data->size` bits (i.e., 1/8th of the intended data) are actually written from the closed captions side data, and the remaining bits in the output are uninitialized/garbage from the bitstream buffer. This causes closed captions data to be garbled/corrupted in the encoded MPEG-2 output. Simply using `side_data->size * 8` would also not work because `ff_copy_bits()` relies on the source buffer being padded (AV_INPUT_BUFFER_PADDING_SIZE), which side_data->data may not satisfy, leading to potential out-of-bounds reads. Root cause: Unit mismatch: ff_copy_bits() expects a bit count for its length parameter, but was passed a byte count (side_data->size). This is a classic unit confusion error introduced during a simplification refactoring.

findings.message: The refactoring in commit 6e225123d replaced a byte-by-byte `put_bits` loop with a single `ff_copy_bits()` call. However, `ff_copy_bits()` expects its third argument `length` to be the number of **bits** to copy (as documented in put_bits.h: '@param length the number of bits of src to copy'). The code passes `side_data->size`, which is a byte count. This means only `side_data->size` bits (i.e., 1/8th of the intended data) are actually written from the closed captions side data, and the remaining bits in the output are uninitialized/garbage from the bitstream buffer. This causes closed captions data to be garbled/corrupted in the encoded MPEG-2 output. Simply using `side_data->size * 8` would also not work because `ff_copy_bits()` relies on the source buffer being padded (AV_INPUT_BUFFER_PADDING_SIZE), which side_data->data may not satisfy, leading to potential out-of-bounds reads.
findings.suggestion: Revert the ff_copy_bits call back to the original byte-by-byte loop using put_bits, since ff_copy_bits expects bit count not byte count, and the side_data buffer may not have the required padding for ff_copy_bits to safely read side_data->size * 8 bits.

agent_reasoning: The bug was in hls_pcm_sample(): the `length` variable—used to determine how many bits to read from the PCM bypass stream—included chroma contributions even when chroma_format_idc == 0 (monochrome/YUV400). For YUV400, hshift and vshift for the chroma planes are both 0, so the chroma size evaluates to 2 * cb_size * cb_size * bit_depth_chroma instead of 0. This inflated `length` caused `skip_bytes()` to consume far more data than actually exists in the PCM block, desynchronising all subsequent bitstream parsing. The fix wraps the chroma terms with a conditional `(sps->chroma_format_idc != 0 ? ... : 0)` so length is correct for monochrome streams. The chroma stride/pointer declarations are also moved inside the `if (sps->chroma_format_idc)` guard to avoid computing invalid pointers into non-existent chroma planes.

pr_description:
When decoding HEVC streams with monochrome (YUV400, chroma_format_idc == 0) content containing PCM-coded blocks, the PCM block bit-length calculation in `hls_pcm_sample()` must exclude any chroma contribution.

This change guards the chroma terms in the `length` computation with `(sps->chroma_format_idc != 0 ? ... : 0)`, so that for YUV400 sequences the length correctly reflects only the luma samples. Correspondingly, the `stride1`/`stride2` and `dst1`/`dst2` variables are moved inside the `if (sps->chroma_format_idc)` block where they are actually used, keeping the chroma-plane pointer arithmetic from being evaluated unnecessarily for monochrome streams.

Without this guard, `skip_bytes()` would advance the bitstream context by far more bytes than are actually present in the PCM payload, desynchronising subsequent CABAC/HEVC parsing and potentially causing out-of-bounds memory accesses downstream.
pr_title: avcodec/hevc: fix PCM block length calculation for monochrome (YUV400) sequences

findings.message: In hls_pcm_sample(), when adding monochrome (YUV400 / chroma_format_idc == 0) support, the put_pcm calls for chroma planes were correctly guarded with `if (s->sps->chroma_format_idc)`, but the `length` calculation was not similarly guarded. For YUV400, hshift and vshift for chroma planes are 0, so the chroma contribution to length becomes `(cb_size * cb_size + cb_size * cb_size) * bit_depth_chroma` instead of 0. This causes `skip_bytes` to skip far more bytes than actually present in the PCM data, leading to incorrect bitstream parsing and corruption of subsequent coding blocks. An attacker could craft a YUV400 HEVC stream with PCM blocks to trigger parsing desynchronization, potentially causing out-of-bounds reads or other memory safety issues downstream.

agent_reasoning: Merged diff composed mechanically by cherry-picking fix 5021764413a1 on top of intro f91906973c62 via git's 3-way merge. Vulnerability (LogicError): The get_eia608_packet function incorrectly assumes that the EIA-608 payload consists of a single 8-byte atom header followed by raw caption byte pairs. In reality, the c608 payload can contain multiple atoms (cdat for CC field 1, cdt2 for CC field 2), each with their own 8-byte header (4 bytes size + 4 bytes type). The function skips only the first 8-byte header via avio_skip(pb, 8) and then treats all remaining bytes as caption data pairs, including the headers of subsequent atoms. This causes: (1) atom headers to be interpreted as caption data, corrupting the output; (2) the hardcoded 0xFC cc_type byte always indicates field 1, so cdt2 (field 2) caption data is misidentified; (3) the size calculation ((size - 8) / 2) * 3 does not account for multiple atom headers, leading to incorrect output buffer sizing. Additionally, there is no integer overflow check on this size calculation — a crafted file with a very large sample size could cause ((size - 8) / 2) * 3 to overflow, resulting in an undersized allocation followed by a heap buffer overflow in the write loop. Root cause: The function was written with the assumption that a c608 sample contains a single atom (one 8-byte header followed by byte pairs), but the actual format allows multiple atoms (cdat, cdt2) each with their own headers. The single avio_skip(pb, 8) only skips the first atom's header, and all subsequent atom headers are misinterpreted as caption data. The hardcoded 0xFC byte also fails to distinguish between CC field 1 and field 2.

findings.message: The get_eia608_packet function incorrectly assumes that the EIA-608 payload consists of a single 8-byte atom header followed by raw caption byte pairs. findings.suggestion: Properly iterate over all atoms in the c608 payload. For each atom, read the 4-byte size and 4-byte type, determine cc_field from the atom type (cdat=field 1, cdt2=field 2), and process only the data portion as caption byte pairs. Set the correct cc_type byte based on the field. Also add an integer overflow check on the size calculation before allocating the output packet.

agent_reasoning: Merged diff composed mechanically by cherry-picking fix 586de322ab7d on top of intro 89828417b062 via git's 3-way merge. Vulnerability (DataRace): In ff_thread_progress_report(), the atomic_store_explicit with memory_order_release is performed OUTSIDE the mutex lock (line 58), before ff_mutex_lock on line 60. This creates a data race when ff_thread_progress_await() takes its slow path (lines 75-78). In the slow path, the awaiting thread holds progress_mutex and reads progress with memory_order_relaxed. If the reporting thread has already done the release-store (line 58) but has not yet acquired the mutex (line 60), the awaiting thread can observe the updated progress value via the relaxed load inside the mutex. However, the relaxed load does not form a proper acquire-release pair with the release store that occurred outside the mutex, so the mutex lock/unlock cannot provide happens-before ordering for the non-atomic shared data (e.g., VP9 motion vectors, decoded block data) written by the reporting thread before calling ff_thread_progress_report(). The awaiting thread may then proceed to read this shared data before the reporting thread's writes are guaranteed visible, causing a data race. ThreadSanitizer confirms this with concurrent read/write accesses to VP9 decoder data (ff_vp9_fill_mv reading, ff_vp9_decode_block writing) across different frame-threading worker threads. Root cause: The atomic_store_explicit(&pro->progress, n, memory_order_release) in ff_thread_progress_report() is placed before ff_mutex_lock(), outside the critical section. In the corresponding ff_thread_progress_await() slow path, the progress is read with memory_order_relaxed inside the mutex. Since the store happened outside the mutex and the load uses relaxed ordering, no proper synchronization (neither acquire-release pair nor mutex happens-before) is established for the non-atomic shared data that the progress value is meant to gate access to.
commit_message:
[Merged] avcodec/threadprogress: Add new API for frame-threaded progress

The API is similar to the ThreadFrame API, with the exception
that it no longer has an included AVFrame and that it has its
own mutexes and condition variables which makes it more independent
of pthread_frame.c. One can wait on anything via a ThreadProgress.
One just has to ensure that the lifetime of the object containing
the ThreadProgress is long enough. This will typically be solved
by putting a ThreadProgress in a refcounted structure that is
shared between threads.

Reviewed-by: Anton Khirnov <anton@khirnov.net>
Reviewed-by: epirat07@gmail.com
Signed-off-by: Andreas Rheinhardt <andreas.rheinhardt@outlook.com>

+{
+    atomic_init(&pro->progress, init_mode ? -1 : INT_MAX);
+#if HAVE_THREADS
+    if (init_mode)
+        return ff_pthread_init(pro, thread_progress_offsets);
+#endif
+    pro->init = init_mode;
+    return 0;
+}
+
+av_cold void ff_thread_progress_destroy(ThreadProgress *pro)
+{
+#if HAVE_THREADS
+    ff_pthread_free(pro, thread_progress_offsets);
+#else
+    pro->init = 0;
+#endif
+}
+
+void ff_thread_progress_report(ThreadProgress *pro, int n)
+{
+    if (atomic_load_explicit(&pro->progress, memory_order_relaxed) >= n)
+        return;
+
+    ff_mutex_lock(&pro->progress_mutex);
+    atomic_store_explicit(&pro->progress, n, memory_order_release);
+    ff_cond_broadcast(&pro->progress_cond);
+    ff_mutex_unlock(&pro->progress_mutex);
+}
+
+void ff_thread_progress_await(const ThreadProgress *pro_c, int n)
+{
+    /* Casting const away here is safe, because we only read from progress
+     * and will leave pro_c in the same state upon leaving the function
+     * as it had at the beginning. */
+    ThreadProgress *pro = (ThreadProgress*)pro_c;
+
+    if (atomic_load_explicit(&pro->progress, memory_order_acquire) >= n)
+        return;
+
+    ff_mutex_lock(&pro->progress_mutex);
+    while (atomic_load_explicit(&pro->progress, memory_order_relaxed) < n)
+        ff_cond_wait(&pro->progress_cond, &pro->progress_mutex);
+    ff_mutex_unlock(&pro->progress_mutex);
+}

+ * License along with FFmpeg; if not, write to the Free Software
+ * Foundation, Inc., 51 Franklin Street, Fifth Floor, Boston, MA 02110-1301 USA
+ */
+
+#ifndef AVCODEC_THREADPROGRESS_H
+#define AVCODEC_THREADPROGRESS_H
+
+/**
+ * ThreadProgress is an API to easily notify other threads about progress
+ * of any kind as long as it can be packaged into an int and is consistent
+ * with the natural ordering of integers.
+ *
+ * Each initialized ThreadProgress can be in one of two modes: No-op mode
+ * or ordinary mode. In the former mode, ff_thread_report_progress() and
+ * ff_thread_await_progress() are no-ops to simply support usecases like
+ * non-frame-threading. Only in the latter case perform these functions
+ * what their name already implies.
+ */
+
+#include <limits.h>
+#include <stdatomic.h>
+#include "libavutil/thread.h"
+
+/**
+ * This struct should be treated as opaque by users.
+ */
+typedef struct ThreadProgress {
+    atomic_int progress;
+    unsigned   init;
+    AVMutex progress_mutex;
+    AVCond  progress_cond;
+} ThreadProgress;
+
+/**
+ * Initialize a ThreadProgress.
+ *
+ * @param init_mode If zero, the ThreadProgress will be initialized
+ *                  to be in no-op mode as described above. Otherwise
+ *                  it is initialized to be in ordinary mode.
+ */
+int ff_thread_progress_init(ThreadProgress *pro, int init_mode);
+
+/**
+ * Destroy a ThreadProgress. Can be called on a ThreadProgress that
+ * has never been initialized provided that the ThreadProgress struct
+ * has been initially zeroed. Must be called even if ff_thread_progress_init()
+ * failed.
+ */
+void ff_thread_progress_destroy(ThreadProgress *pro);
+
+/**
+ * Reset the ::ThreadProgress.progress counter; must only be called
+ * if the ThreadProgress is not in use in any way (e.g. no thread
+ * may wait on it via ff_thread_progress_await()).
+ */
+static inline void ff_thread_progress_reset(ThreadProgress *pro)
+{
+    atomic_init(&pro->progress, pro->init ? -1 : INT_MAX);
+}
+
+/**
+ * This function is a no-op in no-op mode; otherwise it notifies
+ * other threads that a certain level of progress has been reached.
+ * Later calls with lower values of progress have no effect.
+ */
+void ff_thread_progress_report(ThreadProgress *pro, int progress);
+
+/**
+ * This function is a no-op in no-op mode; otherwise it waits
+ * until other threads have reached a certain level of progress:
+ * This function will return after another thread has called
+ * ff_thread_progress_report() with the same or higher value for progress.
+ */
+void ff_thread_progress_await(const ThreadProgress *pro, int progress);
+
+#endif /* AVCODEC_THREADPROGRESS_H */

intro_commit_message:
avcodec/threadprogress: Add new API for frame-threaded progress

The API is similar to the ThreadFrame API, with the exception
that it no longer has an included AVFrame and that it has its
own mutexes and condition variables which makes it more independent
of pthread_frame.c. One can wait on anything via a ThreadProgress.
One just has to ensure that the lifetime of the object containing
the ThreadProgress is long enough. This will typically be solved
by putting a ThreadProgress in a refcounted structure that is
shared between threads.

commit_message:
avcodec/threadprogress: Add new API for frame-threaded progress

The API is similar to the ThreadFrame API, with the exception
that it no longer has an included AVFrame and that it has its
own mutexes and condition variables which makes it more independent
of pthread_frame.c. One can wait on anything via a ThreadProgress.
One just has to ensure that the lifetime of the object containing
the ThreadProgress is long enough. This will typically be solved
by putting a ThreadProgress in a refcounted structure that is
shared between threads.

+
+#include <limits.h>
+#include <stdatomic.h>
+
+#include "pthread_internal.h"
+#include "threadprogress.h"
+#include "libavutil/attributes.h"
+#include "libavutil/thread.h"
+
+DEFINE_OFFSET_ARRAY(ThreadProgress, thread_progress, init,
+                    (offsetof(ThreadProgress, progress_mutex)),
+                    (offsetof(ThreadProgress, progress_cond)));
+
+av_cold int ff_thread_progress_init(ThreadProgress *pro, int init_mode)
+{
+    atomic_init(&pro->progress, init_mode ? -1 : INT_MAX);
+#if HAVE_THREADS
+    if (init_mode)
+        return ff_pthread_init(pro, thread_progress_offsets);
+#endif
+    pro->init = init_mode;
+    return 0;
+}
+
+av_cold void ff_thread_progress_destroy(ThreadProgress *pro)
+{
+#if HAVE_THREADS
+    ff_pthread_free(pro, thread_progress_offsets);
+#else
+    pro->init = 0;
+#endif
+}
+
+void ff_thread_progress_report(ThreadProgress *pro, int n)
+{
+    if (atomic_load_explicit(&pro->progress, memory_order_relaxed) >= n)
+        return;
+
+    atomic_store_explicit(&pro->progress, n, memory_order_release);
+
+    ff_mutex_lock(&pro->progress_mutex);
+    ff_cond_broadcast(&pro->progress_cond);
+    ff_mutex_unlock(&pro->progress_mutex);
+}
+
+void ff_thread_progress_await(const ThreadProgress *pro_c, int n)
+{
+    /* Casting const away here is safe, because we only read from progress
+     * and will leave pro_c in the same state upon leaving the function
+     * as it had at the beginning. */
+    ThreadProgress *pro = (ThreadProgress*)pro_c;
+
+    if (atomic_load_explicit(&pro->progress, memory_order_acquire) >= n)
+        return;
+
+    ff_mutex_lock(&pro->progress_mutex);
+    while (atomic_load_explicit(&pro->progress, memory_order_relaxed) < n)
+        ff_cond_wait(&pro->progress_cond, &pro->progress_mutex);
+    ff_mutex_unlock(&pro->progress_mutex);
+}

+
+#ifndef AVCODEC_THREADPROGRESS_H
+#define AVCODEC_THREADPROGRESS_H
+
+/**
+ * ThreadProgress is an API to easily notify other threads about progress
+ * of any kind as long as it can be packaged into an int and is consistent
+ * with the natural ordering of integers.
+ *
+ * Each initialized ThreadProgress can be in one of two modes: No-op mode
+ * or ordinary mode. In the former mode, ff_thread_report_progress() and
+ * ff_thread_await_progress() are no-ops to simply support usecases like
+ * non-frame-threading. Only in the latter case perform these functions
+ * what their name already implies.
+ */
+
+#include <limits.h>
+#include <stdatomic.h>
+#include "libavutil/thread.h"
+
+/**
+ * This struct should be treated as opaque by users.
+ */
+typedef struct ThreadProgress {
+    atomic_int progress;
+    unsigned   init;
+    AVMutex progress_mutex;
+    AVCond  progress_cond;
+} ThreadProgress;
+
+/**
+ * Initialize a ThreadProgress.
+ *
+ * @param init_mode If zero, the ThreadProgress will be initialized
+ *                  to be in no-op mode as described above. Otherwise
+ *                  it is initialized to be in ordinary mode.
+ */
+int ff_thread_progress_init(ThreadProgress *pro, int init_mode);
+
+/**
+ * Destroy a ThreadProgress. Can be called on a ThreadProgress that
+ * has never been initialized provided that the ThreadProgress struct
+ * has been initially zeroed. Must be called even if ff_thread_progress_init()
+ * failed.
+ */
+void ff_thread_progress_destroy(ThreadProgress *pro);
+
+/**
+ * Reset the ::ThreadProgress.progress counter; must only be called
+ * if the ThreadProgress is not in use in any way (e.g. no thread
+ * may wait on it via ff_thread_progress_await()).
+ */
+static inline void ff_thread_progress_reset(ThreadProgress *pro)
+{
+    atomic_init(&pro->progress, pro->init ? -1 : INT_MAX);
+}
+
+/**
+ * This function is a no-op in no-op mode; otherwise it notifies
+ * other threads that a certain level of progress has been reached.
+ * Later calls with lower values of progress have no effect.
+ */
+void ff_thread_progress_report(ThreadProgress *pro, int progress);
+
+/**
+ * This function is a no-op in no-op mode; otherwise it waits
+ * until other threads have reached a certain level of progress:
+ * This function will return after another thread has called
+ * ff_thread_progress_report() with the same or higher value for progress.
+ */
+void ff_thread_progress_await(const ThreadProgress *pro, int progress);
+
+#endif /* AVCODEC_THREADPROGRESS_H */

findings.message: In ff_thread_progress_report(), the atomic_store_explicit with memory_order_release is performed OUTSIDE the mutex lock (line 58), before ff_mutex_lock on line 60. This creates a data race when ff_thread_progress_await() takes its slow path (lines 75-78). In the slow path, the awaiting thread holds progress_mutex and reads progress with memory_order_relaxed. If the reporting thread has already done the release-store (line 58) but has not yet acquired the mutex (line 60), the awaiting thread can observe the updated progress value via the relaxed load inside the mutex. However, the relaxed load does not form a proper acquire-release pair with the release store that occurred outside the mutex, so the mutex lock/unlock cannot provide happens-before ordering for the non-atomic shared data (e.g., VP9 motion vectors, decoded block data) written by the reporting thread before calling ff_thread_progress_report(). The awaiting thread may then proceed to read this shared data before the reporting thread's writes are guaranteed visible, causing a data race. ThreadSanitizer confirms this with concurrent read/write accesses to VP9 decoder data (ff_vp9_fill_mv reading, ff_vp9_decode_block writing) across different frame-threading worker threads.
findings.suggestion: Move the atomic_store_explicit call inside the mutex lock, so that it is protected by progress_mutex. This ensures that when ff_thread_progress_await's slow path observes the updated progress value under the mutex, the mutex lock/unlock provides the necessary happens-before ordering for all non-atomic shared data written by the reporting thread.

In the corresponding ff_thread_progress_await() slow path, the progress is read with memory_order_relaxed inside the mutex. agent_reasoning: Merged diff composed mechanically by cherry-picking fix 7f9c7f9849a2 on top of intro 80344959f064 via git's 3-way merge. Vulnerability (NullPointerDereference): The `av_freep(&cblk->lengthinc)` call at line 1080 frees the `lengthinc` array and sets the pointer to NULL, but does not reset `cblk->nb_lengthinc` to 0. When `jpeg2000_decode_packet` is called again for the same code block (e.g., across multiple tile parts in a JPEG2000 stream), the stale `nb_lengthinc` value causes the for loop at line 1051 to execute, attempting to dereference the now-NULL `cblk->lengthinc` pointer at line 1052 (`cblk->lengthinc[cwsno]`). The guard at line 1049 (`!cblk->nb_terminationsinc && !cblk->lengthinc`) does not prevent this because `nb_terminationsinc` may be non-zero in a subsequent call, causing the `continue` to be skipped. This results in a SEGV (NULL pointer dereference) that can be triggered by a crafted JPEG2000 file, causing denial of service. Assigned CVE-2025-22921. Root cause: When commit 80344959 added `av_freep(&cblk->lengthinc)` to free the lengthinc array earlier for memory optimization, it neglected to also reset `cblk->nb_lengthinc` to 0. The `av_freep` macro sets the pointer to NULL, but the loop counter remains non-zero, creating an inconsistent state. On a subsequent call to the function for the same code block, the guard condition `!cblk->nb_terminationsinc && !cblk->lengthinc` can be bypassed (when `nb_terminationsinc` is non-zero), and the stale `nb_lengthinc` causes the code to dereference the NULL `lengthinc` pointer.

agent_reasoning: The original `ff_dovi_configure()` created a temporary `AVCodecParameters`, copied the `AVCodecContext` into it with `avcodec_parameters_from_context()`, ran the DOVI configuration logic, then copied everything back with `avcodec_parameters_to_context()`. The `avcodec_parameters_to_context()` call internally frees and replaces `avctx->coded_side_data`, which invalidates any pointers that callers hold into the old `coded_side_data` array (e.g., an `AVCPBProperties *` obtained via `ff_encode_add_cpb_side_data()` before calling `ff_dovi_configure()`). Writing through such a dangling pointer is a heap-use-after-free. The fixed code passes individual fields from `AVCodecContext` directly to the internal helper and writes the resulting DOVI configuration record straight into `avctx->coded_side_data` — no copy-back, no freeing of existing side data, no dangling pointers.

findings.message: ff_dovi_configure() round-trips through an intermediate AVCodecParameters by calling avcodec_parameters_from_context() and then avcodec_parameters_to_context(). The call to avcodec_parameters_to_context(avctx, codecpar) at line 226 internally calls av_packet_side_data_free(&codec->coded_side_data, &codec->nb_coded_side_data), which frees ALL existing coded_side_data entries on the AVCodecContext (including any AVCPBProperties previously allocated via ff_encode_add_cpb_side_data()). It then replaces coded_side_data with a copy from the intermediate codecpar. Any caller that holds a pointer into the old coded_side_data (e.g., cpb_props in libaomenc.c obtained before calling ff_dovi_configure) now has a dangling pointer, leading to a heap-use-after-free when that pointer is subsequently written to.
findings.suggestion: Avoid the round-trip through AVCodecParameters entirely. Instead, pass the individual fields from AVCodecContext directly to the configuration function, and write side data directly to avctx->coded_side_data rather than going through an intermediate codecpar that triggers free+copy of the context's side data.

agent_reasoning: The vulnerability was a NULL pointer dereference in `unpack_dct_coeffs()`. After the frame-threading refactor changed `submit_packet()` to no longer be a no-op during draining for no-delay codecs, `prev_thread` could be set to a worker thread that was never initialized with VLC tables. When flushing occurred, `vp3_update_thread_context()` would copy that NULL `coeff_vlc` to the first decode thread via `av_refstruct_replace()`. On the next decode attempt, dereferencing `s->coeff_vlc` caused a SIGSEGV. The fix avoids this entirely by initializing the VLCs once during `vp3_decode_init()` using `ff_thread_sync_ref()` (which returns `FF_THREAD_IS_COPY` for worker threads, skipping re-initialization) and removing the per-frame sync from `vp3_update_thread_context()`. This means the VLCs are always valid for any thread that has completed init, regardless of flushing or threading state.
commit_message:
[Merged] lavc: convert frame threading to the receive_frame() pattern

Reorganize the code such that the frame threading code does not call the
decoders directly, but instead calls back into the generic decoding
code. This avoids duplicating the logic that wraps the decoder
invocation and allows receive_frame()-based decoders to use frame
threading.

Further work by Timo Rothenpieler <timo@rothenpieler.org>.

fix_commit_message:
avcodec/vp3: Sync VLCs once during init, fix crash

6c7a344b65cb7476d1575cb1504e3a53bcbc83e7 made the VLCs shared between
threads and did so in a way that was designed to support stream
reconfigurations, so that the structure containing the VLCs was
synced in update_thread_context. The idea was that the currently
active VLCs would just be passed along between threads.

Yet this was broken by 5acbdd2264d3b90dc11369f9e031e762f260882e:
Before this commit, submit_packet() was a no-op during flushing
for VP3, as it is a no-delay decoder, so it won't produce any output
during flushing. This meant that prev_thread in pthread_frame.c
contained the last dst thread that update_thread_context()
was called for (so that these VLCs could be passed along between
threads). Yet after said commit, submit_packet was no longer
a no-op during flushing and changed prev_thread in such a way
that it did not need to contain any VLCs at all*. When flushing,
prev_thread is used to pass the current state to the first worker
thread which is the one that is used to restart decoding.
It could therefore happen that the decoding thread did not contain
the VLCs at all any more after decoding restarts after flushing
leading to a crash (this scenario was never anticipated and
must not happen at all).

There is a simple, easily backportable fix given that we do not
support stream reconfigurations (yet) when using frame threading:
Don't sync the VLCs in update_thread_context(), instead do it once
during init.

This fixes forgejo issue #20346 and trac issue #11592.

(I don't know why 5acbdd2264d3b90dc11369f9e031e762f260882e
changed submit_packet() to no longer be a no-op when draining
no-delay decoders.)

*: The exact condition for the crash is nb_threads > 2*nb_frames.

Reviewed-by: Peter Ross <pross@xvid.org>
Signed-off-by: Andreas Rheinhardt <andreas.rheinhardt@outlook.com>

intro_commit_message:
lavc: convert frame threading to the receive_frame() pattern

Reorganize the code such that the frame threading code does not call the
decoders directly, but instead calls back into the generic decoding
code. This avoids duplicating the logic that wraps the decoder
invocation and allows receive_frame()-based decoders to use frame
threading.

Further work by Timo Rothenpieler <timo@rothenpieler.org>.
pr_description:
When using frame threading with VP3/Theora, the coefficient VLC tables are shared across decoder threads via a reference-counted structure. Previously, the primary thread was identified using `avctx->internal->is_copy`, and the VLCs were re-synced between threads in `vp3_update_thread_context()` on every frame.

This approach is fragile: `update_thread_context` does not always run in a predictable order relative to flushing, and relying on VLC propagation through the thread context chain means a thread that never decoded a frame can end up with a NULL `coeff_vlc` pointer, causing a crash when decoding resumes after a flush (e.g. a seek).

This commit switches to the cleaner `ff_thread_sync_ref()` API introduced for this purpose. The VLCs are now allocated and initialized exactly once — on the first (non-copy) thread during `vp3_decode_init()` — and the reference is automatically shared to all worker threads by the threading framework. The `av_refstruct_replace()` call in `vp3_update_thread_context()` is removed, since the framework handles the initial ref-copy and there is no need to re-sync on every frame.

The `internal.h` include is no longer needed after removing the `is_copy` check and is dropped.
pr_title: avcodec/vp3: Initialize VLCs once during init using ff_thread_sync_ref

findings.message: The refactoring of submit_packet() removed the early return for no-delay codecs (`if (!avpkt->size && !(codec->capabilities & AV_CODEC_CAP_DELAY)) return 0;`). The replacement guard at lines 537-538 only skips `update_context_from_thread()` during draining for no-delay codecs, but the function still proceeds to set `fctx->prev_thread = p` at line 559, pointing it to a thread that was never initialized with VLCs (coeff_vlc). When nb_threads > 2*nb_frames, prev_thread ends up pointing to a thread that never decoded anything. On the next call to ff_thread_flush(), line 991 copies context from this VLC-less prev_thread to thread[0] via update_context_from_thread(), which calls vp3_update_thread_context() and sets coeff_vlc to NULL via av_refstruct_replace(). When decoding then restarts, unpack_dct_coeffs() at vp3.c:1301 dereferences the NULL coeff_vlc pointer, causing a SIGSEGV.
findings.suggestion: Either restore the early return in submit_packet() for no-delay codecs during draining (`if (!avpkt->size && !(codec->capabilities & AV_CODEC_CAP_DELAY)) return 0;`), or move VLC synchronization out of update_thread_context into the codec init function so VLCs are set once during initialization and not dependent on prev_thread propagation. The fix commit chose the latter approach: syncing VLCs once during init via ff_thread_sync_ref() and removing the av_refstruct_replace(&s->coeff_vlc, s1->coeff_vlc) call from vp3_update_thread_context().

agent_reasoning: Merged diff composed mechanically by cherry-picking fix b8d5f65b9e89 on top of intro af052f9066a1 via git's 3-way merge. Vulnerability (DoubleFree): ff_dnn_execute_model_tf() in libavfilter/dnn/dnn_backend_tf.c allocates a TaskItem and pushes it into tf_model->task_queue. After the push succeeds, the queue owns the TaskItem and it will be freed later by dnn_free_model_tf() when the DNN model is torn down. Commit af052f9066 ('lavfi/dnn: fix mem leak in TF backend error handle'), while fixing a genuine leak for the pre-push error paths, incorrectly also added av_freep(&task) calls to the two error branches that run after the successful push_back call (failure of extract_lltask_from_task() and failure to obtain a request from request_queue). Because the task remains referenced in task_queue, it gets freed again during model cleanup, causing a double free / heap corruption. Root cause: The fix for a memory leak did not track that ownership of 'task' had already transferred to tf_model->task_queue after a successful ff_queue_push_back() call, so it freed the same object both immediately in the error path and later during queue teardown in dnn_free_model_tf().

findings.message: In ff_dnn_execute_model_tf(), after the TaskItem 'task' is successfully pushed onto tf_model->task_queue via ff_queue_push_back(), ownership of 'task' is transferred to the queue. dnn_free_model_tf() later walks tf_model->task_queue and calls av_freep() on every queued item when the model is freed. However, this commit (intended to fix a memory leak in earlier error paths) added av_freep(&task) calls in the two error branches that execute AFTER the successful ff_queue_push_back(task) call: the extract_lltask_from_task() failure branch and the ff_safe_queue_pop_front(request_queue) failure branch. Since 'task' remains linked in task_queue in both cases, it will be freed a second time when dnn_free_model_tf() (invoked during filter teardown / ff_dnn_uninit) walks and frees the queue, resulting in a double free of the TaskItem.
findings.suggestion: Do not call av_freep(&task) in error branches that occur after 'task' has already been successfully queued into tf_model->task_queue via ff_queue_push_back(). Once queued, ownership belongs to the queue and dnn_free_model_tf()/model teardown will free it. Only free 'task' directly in error paths that occur BEFORE it is pushed to the queue (e.g., the ff_dnn_fill_task failure and the ff_queue_push_back failure itself).

findings.message: In dump_stream_group(), when printing a AV_STREAM_GROUP_PARAMS_TILE_GRID group, the code iterates `for (int i = 0; i < tile_grid->nb_tiles; i++)` and uses `tile_grid->offsets[i].idx` as an index into `stg->streams[]` (`stg->streams[tile_grid->offsets[i].idx]`). The number of tiles (`tile_grid->nb_tiles`) is not guaranteed to match, or be bounded by, the number of streams actually present in the stream group (`stg->nb_streams`). A tile grid can reference (via `offsets[i].idx`) an index that is out of range for the `stg->streams` array, or the loop itself may simply not correspond 1:1 with valid stream entries, leading to an out-of-bounds read of the `stg->streams` array and subsequent dereference of an invalid/garbage `AVStream *` pointer (`st->index`, `dump_stream_format`, `printed[st->index]`). This can be triggered by a maliciously crafted/malformed file (e.g. AVIF/HEIF tile grid) whose declared tile count or tile indices are inconsistent with the actual number of streams in the group, causing FFmpeg's `ffprobe`/`-dump_format` (or any consumer that dumps stream group information) to read out of bounds and potentially crash or leak memory.
findings.suggestion: Do not trust `tile_grid->nb_tiles` / `tile_grid->offsets[i].idx` as bounded indices into `stg->streams[]`. Instead iterate over `stg->nb_streams` (the actual, validated number of streams in the group) directly and index `stg->streams[i]`, as done in the fix. If per-tile info still needs to be shown, validate `offsets[i].idx` against `stg->nb_streams` before using it as an array index.

agent_reasoning: The intro commit introduced backward-scanning logic in get_duration() that computes end_pos from an attacker-controlled seek_back value read from the file. The validation only checked end_pos < 0 rather than end_pos < end_buffer_pos, which is the actual lower bound of the allocated buffer since end_buffer_pos can be a large positive offset. commit_message:
avformat/dhav: fix backward scanning for get_duration and optimize seeking

The backwards scanning done for incomplete final packets should not
assume a specific alignment at the end of the file. Truncated files
result in hundreds of thousands of seeks if the final packet does not
fall on a specific byte boundary, which can be extremely slow.
For example, with HTTP, each backwards seek results in a separate
HTTP request.

This changes the scanning to check for the end tag 1 byte at a time
and buffers the last 1 MiB to avoid additional seek operations.

findings.message: In get_duration(), a backward scan of a 1MiB buffer (end_buffer, spanning file offsets [end_buffer_pos, end_buffer_pos+end_buffer_size)) computes a candidate reference position end_pos = end_buffer_pos + offset - seek_back + 8, where seek_back is an attacker-controlled 32-bit value read directly from the file. Because seek_back can be arbitrarily large, end_pos can end up smaller than end_buffer_pos (i.e. before the start of the allocated buffer), while still remaining >= 0 (or even becoming negative if inputs align just right). The validation check `if (end_pos < 0 || end_pos + 16 > end_buffer_pos + end_buffer_size)` only rejects negative end_pos and enforces an upper bound relative to the buffer end, but it fails to verify `end_pos >= end_buffer_pos`. As a result, a crafted dhav file can cause `end_buffer + (end_pos - end_buffer_pos) + 16` to compute a pointer far before the beginning of `end_buffer`, and the subsequent AV_RL32() read at that pointer becomes an out-of-bounds heap read on the allocated end_buffer array.
findings.suggestion: Validate end_pos against both bounds of the allocated buffer, not just against zero: require end_pos to be at least end_buffer_pos before computing the offset into end_buffer, in addition to the existing upper-bound check.
findings.title: Out-of-bounds read due to insufficient lower-bound check on end_pos in get_duration()

fix_commit.message: avformat/dhav: fix reference point mixup

must_cover.reason: Primary location of finding: Out-of-bounds read due to insufficient lower-bound check on end_pos in get_duration()

ground_truth.root_cause: The bounds check after computing end_pos from an attacker-controlled seek_back value validated only the negative/zero boundary condition (`end_pos < 0`) and the upper-bound condition, but omitted verifying that end_pos was not less than end_buffer_pos, the actual base offset of the allocated buffer. Since end_pos is derived by subtracting an untrusted 32-bit seek_back from an in-buffer offset, it can easily fall below end_buffer_pos without becoming negative overall (since offsets are int64_t and end_buffer_pos can be large), allowing an out-of-bounds pointer to be dereferenced.

Adds a decoder for the SMUSH codec48 video encoding, as is used by
the LucasArts game "Mysteries of the Sith".

findings.message: The old_codec48() function reads a 32-bit `decoded_size` value directly from the bitstream (`uint32_t decoded_size = bytestream2_get_le32(&ctx->gb);`) and, when compr == 2, passes it unvalidated as the output length to rle_decode(), which writes `decoded_size` bytes into the fixed-size frame buffer `dst` (ctx->frm0). Because `decoded_size` is fully attacker-controlled and is never compared against the actual size of the destination buffer (ctx->buf_size / the frame allocation based on width*height), a crafted SANM/SMUSH codec48 frame can specify a decoded_size far larger than the buffer, causing rle_decode() to write past the end of the frame buffer (heap buffer overflow / out-of-bounds write). This was found by Google Big Sleep and fixed in commit 3ccd7d8c8e85aaae0c6d6cc88ea6cb5309d56cdc by adding a check that rejects decoded_size values greater than ctx->buf_size before calling rle_decode().
findings.suggestion: Validate decoded_size against the known bounds of the destination buffer (e.g., ctx->buf_size, or width*height/aligned_height) before invoking rle_decode(), and return AVERROR_INVALIDDATA if the value is too large, mirroring the checks already used for the compr==0 and compr==5 branches in the same function.
findings.title: Missing bounds check on attacker-controlled decoded_size in old_codec48 RLE path

findings.message: dwa_uncompress() reads the 64-bit field rle_raw_size directly from the compressed EXR bitstream and later uses it to compute offsets into the rle_raw_data buffer (`td->rle_raw_data + y * td->xsize + rle_raw_size / 2`) inside a loop that iterates td->ysize times and td->xsize times per row. The buffer td->rle_raw_data is allocated with exactly rle_raw_size bytes (via av_fast_padded_malloc), but the code never verifies that rle_raw_size is large enough to cover `2 * td->xsize * td->ysize` bytes (the amount actually accessed by the ai0/ai1 pointers across the full loop), nor that rle_raw_size fits within a sane/non-overflowing range (it's read as int64_t and can be attacker controlled up to 2^63-1, later truncated/misused as unsigned/int in allocation and pointer arithmetic). A small or otherwise inconsistent rle_raw_size relative to td->xsize/td->ysize (which are also attacker influenced) lets ai0/ai1 index far past the end of the allocated rle_raw_data buffer, causing an out-of-bounds heap read that leaks adjacent heap memory into the decoded pixel data. This was reported by Google Big Sleep as BIGSLEEP-436510153/dwa_uncompress_read.exr.
findings.suggestion: Before allocating/using rle_raw_data, validate that rle_raw_size is within sane bounds (e.g. reject if it exceeds INT_MAX) and, critically, verify that rle_raw_size is at least `2 * td->xsize * td->ysize` (the maximum offset accessed by ai0/ai1 in the following read loop) before entering the loop that dereferences ai0/ai1. Reject the frame with AVERROR_INVALIDDATA if these invariants do not hold, as later done in commit 0d9c003d76383e82b57b6d5aa33776709d0cda2c.

agent_reasoning: Merged diff composed mechanically by cherry-picking fix f7cc023f06c4 on top of intro 649ac17efd96 via git's 3-way merge. Vulnerability (IntegerOverflow): In FFmpeg's MXF demuxer, mxf_edit_unit_absolute_offset() rescales and clamps a caller-supplied edit_unit value against the bounds of the index table's first/last segments. findings.message: In mxf_edit_unit_absolute_offset(), after edit_unit is rescaled via av_rescale_q() it is clamped with `edit_unit = FFMAX(FFMIN(edit_unit, index_end), first_segment->index_start_position);`. This clamp does not guarantee edit_unit is non-negative: if first_segment->index_start_position itself is a huge negative value (attacker-controlled via a crafted MXF index table segment), edit_unit can remain an extremely large negative int64 value (e.g. close to INT64_MIN). This value then flows into the segment-search loop where `int64_t index = edit_unit - s->index_start_position;` is computed and, for VBR/Avid indexes, `index *= 2;` is executed when `s->nb_index_entries == 2 * s->index_duration + 1`. Multiplying a value close to INT64_MIN by 2 causes signed integer overflow (undefined behavior), as reported by UBSan fuzzing ('signed integer overflow: 2 * -4962931467012268000 cannot be represented in type long'). The function lacks a check that edit_unit remains within a sane, non-negative range after clamping before it is used in further arithmetic.
findings.suggestion: After clamping edit_unit to the index range, explicitly reject negative values before using edit_unit in further arithmetic (index computation, doubling for Avid indexes, etc.), since a crafted MXF file can make first_segment->index_start_position an extremely large negative number that survives the FFMAX/FFMIN clamp.

agent_reasoning: Merged diff composed mechanically by cherry-picking fix 02958ab7156b on top of intro 9cfc7a244052 via git's 3-way merge. Vulnerability (IntegerOverflow): libavformat/mov.c's mov_read_stts() parses the 'stts' (sample-to-time / time-to-sample) box in MOV/MP4 files, tracking two int64_t accumulators, current_dts and corrected_dts, derived from file-supplied 32-bit sample_count and sample_duration values (including a max_stts_delta correction path that reinterprets large unsigned durations as signed int32 deltas). When these two accumulators diverge to very large values of opposite sign after processing many crafted stts entries, the plain signed subtraction 'current_dts - corrected_dts' used to compute a drift correction can overflow int64_t, which is undefined behavior in C. OSS-Fuzz's UndefinedBehaviorSanitizer flagged this while fuzzing the media pipeline integration fuzzer. Root cause: The max_stts_delta feature (added in commit 9cfc7a2440) introduced accumulation of two independently-growing int64_t DTS trackers (current_dts, corrected_dts) driven directly by untrusted 32-bit file fields, and then performed unchecked signed subtraction between them to derive a 'drift' correction value without validating that the operands stay within a range where the subtraction cannot overflow int64_t.
commit_message:
avformat/mov: add option max_stts_delta

Very high stts sample deltas may occasionally be intended but usually
they are written in error or used to store a negative value for dts correction
when treated as signed 32-bit integers.

This option lets the user set an upper limit, beyond which the delta is clamped to 1.
Values greater than the limit if negative when cast to int32 are used to adjust onward dts.

Unit is the track time scale. Default is UINT_MAX - 48000*10 which
allows upto a 10 second dts correction for 48 kHz audio streams while
accommodating 99.9% of uint32 range.

Signed-off-by: Gyan Doshi <ffmpeg@gyani.pro>
Reviewed-by: Michael Niedermayer <michael@niedermayer.cc>

commit_message:
avformat/mov: add option max_stts_delta

Very high stts sample deltas may occasionally be intended but usually
they are written in error or used to store a negative value for dts correction
when treated as signed 32-bit integers.

This option lets the user set an upper limit, beyond which the delta is clamped to 1.
Values greater than the limit if negative when cast to int32 are used to adjust onward dts.

Unit is the track time scale. Default is UINT_MAX - 48000*10 which
allows upto a 10 second dts correction for 48 kHz audio streams while
accommodating 99.9% of uint32 range.

Signed-off-by: Gyan Doshi <ffmpeg@gyani.pro>
Reviewed-by: Michael Niedermayer <michael@niedermayer.cc>

findings.message: In mov_read_stts(), when processing the 'stts' (sample-to-time) atom, the code accumulates current_dts and corrected_dts as int64_t values based on attacker/file-controlled sample_duration and sample_count fields. When current_dts exceeds corrected_dts, the code computes 'drift = (current_dts - corrected_dts) / FFMAX(sample_count, 1)' using plain signed subtraction. Because corrected_dts can be adjusted by a large negative delta_magnitude derived from a crafted 32-bit sample_duration value cast to int32_t, and current_dts can independently grow very large from repeated large sample_duration*sample_count accumulations across many stts entries, the two accumulators can end up with extreme, oppositely-signed magnitudes (e.g. ~7.8e18 minus ~-3.4e18). The subtraction 'current_dts - corrected_dts' then overflows the range of int64_t, which is undefined behavior in C and was caught by UBSan/OSS-Fuzz (signed integer overflow: 7803923888585309955 - -3407677434275325337 cannot be represented in type 'int64_t'). This is reachable purely by supplying a crafted MOV/MP4 file with pathological stts entries, with no other preconditions.
findings.suggestion: Use a saturating/overflow-safe subtraction primitive (e.g. FFmpeg's av_sat_sub64()) instead of plain '-' when computing the difference between current_dts and corrected_dts, since both are derived from untrusted, attacker-controlled file data and can reach extreme magnitudes of opposite sign.
findings.suggestion_code: int64_t drift = av_sat_sub64(current_dts, corrected_dts) / FFMAX(sample_count, 1);
findings.title: Signed integer overflow in STTS drift calculation (current_dts - corrected_dts)

fix_commit.author: James Almer
fix_commit.message: avformat/mov: fix overflow in drift timestamp calculation

must_cover.reason: Primary location of finding: Signed integer overflow in STTS drift calculation (current_dts - corrected_dts)

ground_truth.root_cause: The max_stts_delta feature (added in commit 9cfc7a2440) introduced accumulation of two independently-growing int64_t DTS trackers (current_dts, corrected_dts) driven directly by untrusted 32-bit file fields, and then performed unchecked signed subtraction between them to derive a 'drift' correction value without validating that the operands stay within a range where the subtraction cannot overflow int64_t.

agent_reasoning: The bug-introducing commit added a heuristic to correct broken block_align values in W64 files by computing a minimum expected block_align from bits_per_coded_sample and channel count, using 32-bit int arithmetic. Both operands are attacker-controlled, so the multiplication can overflow a signed int (UB), as found by OSS-Fuzz. The fix commit widens the intermediate computation to 64-bit by declaring the local `block_align` variable as `int64_t` and using a `7LL` literal to force 64-bit division/multiplication. I applied the equivalent minimal edit directly to the corresponding lines in the worktree's w64_read_header function (which lacks the unrelated FF_SANE_NB_CHANNELS condition present in the fix's context, since that's not part of this bug's introduction), preserving the rest of the logic unchanged.

avformat/wavdec: w64: do not error out for broken files if data start is found

Also attempt to fix invalid block_align value.

findings.message: In w64_read_header(), when parsing the 'fmt ' chunk, the code attempts to sanity-check and possibly correct an invalid block_align value read from the file. The check computes `((bits_per_coded_sample + 7) / 8) * ch_layout.nb_channels` using plain `int` arithmetic and stores the result into a local `int block_align`. Because `bits_per_coded_sample` and `nb_channels` are attacker-controlled values parsed from the file (via ff_get_wav_header), this multiplication can overflow a 32-bit signed int (undefined behavior in C, and in practice produces a negative/incorrect value with -fsanitize=undefined flagging it, e.g. '-251517880 * 32 cannot be represented in type int'). The resulting corrupted/undefined value is then compared against and potentially assigned into st->codecpar->block_align, defeating the purpose of the sanity check and potentially leaving block_align inconsistent with the true per-sample data size, which downstream code relies on for buffer size / stride calculations.
findings.suggestion: Perform the intermediate multiplication used in the block_align sanity check using a wide (64-bit) integer type to avoid signed overflow, matching the eventual fix: declare block_align as int64_t and use a 64-bit literal (7LL) in the bits_per_coded_sample rounding computation before multiplying by ch_layout.nb_channels.
findings.title: Signed integer overflow in block_align sanity check for W64/WAV demuxer

agent_reasoning: Merged diff composed mechanically by cherry-picking fix a50d36b5fd39 on top of intro 8eb1d76e146a via git's 3-way merge. Vulnerability (NullPointerDereference): The VVC decoder's set_pict_type() function, added to export a frame's picture type (I/P/B) and keyframe flag, scans the current access unit's coded bitstream (CBS) units for slice NAL units and inspects their parsed slice header (content_ref) to determine whether the frame contains inter or B slices. The loop only checked unit->type against VVC_RSV_IRAP_11 but did not verify that unit->content_ref was actually non-NULL before dereferencing it as an H266RawSliceHeader pointer within the IS_I/IS_B macros. Malformed input can produce a unit with a slice-type NAL unit type but a NULL content_ref, leading to a crash. Root cause: Missing NULL check on unit->content_ref before dereferencing it as a parsed slice header structure; the code assumed that any CBS unit with a slice-like NAL unit type would always have its content_ref populated, which is not guaranteed for malformed/incompletely parsed bitstreams.

findings.message: In set_pict_type(), when determining the picture type for a VVC frame, the code iterates over the CodedBitstreamUnit array of the current access unit and, for every unit whose type is <= VVC_RSV_IRAP_11 (i.e. a slice NAL unit), directly dereferences unit->content_ref as an H266RawSliceHeader* without first checking that content_ref is non-NULL. The CBS layer does not guarantee that content_ref has been populated for every unit with a slice NAL unit type at this point in decoding (e.g. malformed/truncated bitstreams can produce slice-type units whose content has not been parsed/attached yet). When content_ref is NULL, IS_I(rsh) and IS_B(rsh) dereference a NULL H266RawSliceHeader pointer, causing a NULL pointer dereference crash. This was found by OSS-Fuzz (clusterfuzz testcase for the VVC fuzzer).
findings.suggestion: Check that unit->content_ref is non-NULL before treating it as a valid H266RawSliceHeader pointer and dereferencing it via IS_I/IS_B macros.
findings.title: NULL pointer dereference in set_pict_type() via unit->content_ref

agent_reasoning: Merged diff composed mechanically by cherry-picking fix 43926e026dd8 on top of intro 63ea1660fa06 via git's 3-way merge. Vulnerability (BufferOverflow): In FFmpeg's American Laser Games MM video decoder (libavcodec/mmvideo.c), the mm_decode_pal() function reads a 16-bit 'start' offset and a 16-bit 'count' value directly from the input bitstream and uses them, unvalidated, as the base index and loop bound for writing entries into the fixed-size s->palette[AVPALETTE_COUNT] (256-entry) array. Because neither value is bounds-checked against the array size, a maliciously crafted MM video file can cause the decoder to write palette entries far outside the bounds of the palette array, resulting in an out-of-bounds write detected by OSS-Fuzz (clusterfuzz-testcase-minimized-ffmpeg_AV_CODEC_ID_MMVIDEO_fuzzer-4655048979709952). Root cause: The refactor in commit 63ea1660fa ("avcodec/mm: decode partial palette") replaced a previous fixed 128-iteration loop with a stream-controlled 'start' offset and 'count' loop bound, but failed to mask/clamp the resulting array index (start+i) to the valid range of the palette array, allowing attacker-controlled values to index arbitrarily far outside the array.

commit_message: avcodec/mm: decode partial palette

findings.message: mm_decode_pal() reads a 16-bit 'start' offset and a 16-bit 'count' directly from the bitstream (both attacker-controlled, up to 65535) and then writes 'count' consecutive unsigned ints into s->palette[start+i] without ever validating that start+i stays within the bounds of the palette array (unsigned int palette[AVPALETTE_COUNT], i.e. 256 entries). Because bytestream2_get_le16() imposes no limit on the returned value, an attacker-crafted MM video stream can supply start and/or count values large enough to make start+i exceed 255, causing writes far past the end of the MmContext::palette array. This is a heap/struct out-of-bounds write (the OSS-Fuzz report calls it out-of-array access), which can corrupt adjacent heap memory and potentially lead to memory corruption or code execution.
findings.suggestion: Mask or clamp the palette write index to the valid range of the palette array (0..AVPALETTE_COUNT-1), e.g. by ANDing (start+i) with 0xFF as done in the actual fix, or by validating that start and count keep start+i within bounds before performing the write, and rejecting/truncating the loop otherwise.
findings.title: Out-of-bounds write in mm_decode_pal via unchecked start+i palette index

agent_reasoning: Merged diff composed mechanically by cherry-picking fix 251d43aef0df on top of intro 86dd15fd0dd0 via git's 3-way merge. Vulnerability (IntegerOverflow): The MLV demuxer's LJ92 frame-decoding path (added to support demuxing LJ92 huffman-compressed frames) computes a packet payload `size` from attacker-controlled fields in the MLV bitstream (block size, timestamp/frame fields, optional crop/pan fields for video, and a variable-length `space` field) without sufficiently validating that the resulting value is non-negative/in-range. This unchecked `size` is then used both to allocate a packet buffer (`av_new_packet(pkt, size + MAX_HEADER_SIZE)`) and to read that many bytes into it (`avio_read(pbio, pkt->data + header_size, size)`), and separately to compute the audio packet length. A crafted MLV file can cause `size` to underflow (since `size` is an unsigned int subtracted by attacker-controlled `space`) or otherwise reach values that make `size + MAX_HEADER_SIZE` overflow, resulting in a heap buffer overflow when the actual read/allocate sizes disagree. Root cause: Missing/insufficient bounds validation on an attacker-controlled `size` (and the related `space` field) before it is used in unsigned arithmetic (subtraction that can underflow) and in a size-plus-constant allocation (addition that can overflow), both feeding directly into memory allocation and copy operations.
commit_message:
avformat/mlvdec: demux LJ92 huffman comressed frames

A minimal DNG header is added to each LJ92 compressed frame, allowing
thme to be decoded by the TIFF decoder. The TIFF decoder is responsible
for setting up the MJPEG decoder, signalling the correct s->bayer flag,
and setting pix_fmt.

The LJ92 compressed frames can be muxed out to DNG files, and manipulated
in DNG software. Tested with darktable and rawtherapee.

commit_message:
avformat/mlvdec: demux LJ92 huffman comressed frames

A minimal DNG header is added to each LJ92 compressed frame, allowing
thme to be decoded by the TIFF decoder. The TIFF decoder is responsible
for setting up the MJPEG decoder, signalling the correct s->bayer flag,
and setting pix_fmt.

The LJ92 compressed frames can be muxed out to DNG files, and manipulated

Contributor: South East <8billion.people@gmail.com>

findings.message: get_packet_lj92() takes a 64-bit `size` value that is derived, in read_packet(), from an unsigned 32-bit value read straight from the MLV file (block size minus a few fixed header fields and an attacker-controlled `space` field). Neither read_packet() nor get_packet_lj92() validates that `size` is within a sane range before it is used. Inside get_packet_lj92(), the packet buffer is allocated with `av_new_packet(pkt, size + MAX_HEADER_SIZE)`. Because `size` is attacker-controlled and unchecked, `size + MAX_HEADER_SIZE` can overflow (or otherwise not match the amount actually written), and the subsequent `avio_read(pbio, pkt->data + header_size, size)` can then write `size` bytes past the end of the allocated packet buffer, causing a heap-buffer-overflow. Additionally, in read_packet(), `size` is decremented by fixed amounts (12, optionally 8) and by the attacker-controlled `space` value (`size -= space;`) without first checking that `size` is large enough, allowing an unsigned underflow that produces a huge `size` value which is then passed straight into get_packet_lj92() or used for the audio packet size calculation.
findings.suggestion: Validate the `size` value before it is used to allocate/copy memory. In get_packet_lj92(), reject sizes that would overflow the allocation (e.g. `if ((uint64_t)size > INT32_MAX - MAX_HEADER_SIZE) return AVERROR_PATCHWELCOME;` before calling av_new_packet). In read_packet(), check that `size` is large enough before each subtraction (e.g. verify `size >= 8` before subtracting the crop/pan fields, and `size >= space + 4` before subtracting `space`) so that the unsigned `size` variable cannot underflow to a huge value that is later passed into get_packet_lj92() or used to compute the audio packet length.
findings.title: Unchecked attacker-controlled `size` leads to integer overflow and heap-buffer-overflow in get_packet_lj92()

agent_reasoning: Merged diff composed mechanically by cherry-picking fix d643a5ba0836 on top of intro 11a8e0a4e585 via git's 3-way merge. Vulnerability (OutOfBoundsRead): In the FFmpeg USAC/xHE-AAC decoder's noise-filling logic (apply_noise_fill in libavcodec/aac/aacdec_usac.c), an integer offset derived from the bitstream (noise_offset = ue->noise.offset - 16) is added unconditionally to sce->sfo[], the raw scalefactor offset array. This array element is later used, without further validation, as an index (after an additive constant POW_SF2_ZERO) into the fixed-size table ff_aac_pow2sf_tab in dequant_scalefactors(). Because the accumulation into sfo is unbounded, a maliciously crafted AAC LATM/USAC bitstream can drive sfo to a value negative enough that the resulting table index is out of bounds, leading to an out-of-bounds read. Root cause: A refactor moved the noise-offset application from the dequantized float scalefactor (sce->sf, which was numerically safe to add an offset to) onto the raw integer scalefactor-offset value (sce->sfo) that is later used directly as an array index/lookup-table offset, without adding any bounds clamp on the new value. The bitstream-controlled noise.offset field combined with repeated/attacker-influenced sfo values allowed the stored offset to become large enough to index outside the pow2sf lookup table.
commit_message:
aacdec_usac: dequantize scalefactors after noise synthesis

The issue here is that the spec implied that the offset is done
on the dequantized scalefactor, but in fact, it is done on the
scalefactor offset. Delay dequantizing the scalefactors until
after noise synthesis is performed, and change to apply the
offset onto the offset.

aacdec_usac: dequantize scalefactors after noise synthesis

The issue here is that the spec implied that the offset is done
on the dequantized scalefactor, but in fact, it is done on the
scalefactor offset. Delay dequantizing the scalefactors until

findings.message: In apply_noise_fill(), when a scalefactor band is fully quantized to zero and noise filling is applied, the code adds noise_offset (derived from ue->noise.offset - 16, an 8-bit field that ranges roughly -16..15) directly onto sce->sfo[g*ics->max_sfb + sfb] with no lower-bound clamp: `sce->sfo[g*ics->max_sfb + sfb] += noise_offset;`. This commit changed the target of the offset from sce->sf (a floating point *dequantized* scalefactor, which was safe to arbitrarily offset) to sce->sfo (the raw integer scalefactor index/offset). sfo is later used directly as an index into fixed-size lookup tables in dequant_scalefactors() (aacdec_dsp_template.c), e.g. `ff_aac_pow2sf_tab[-sfo[idx] - 100 + POW_SF2_ZERO]` and `ff_aac_pow2sf_tab[sfo[idx] + POW_SF2_ZERO]`. Because apply_noise_fill() can be invoked multiple times or sce->sfo can already start at an extreme value from bitstream-controlled scalefactor deltas, and because there is no clamp on sfo after applying noise_offset, an attacker-controlled bitstream can drive sfo far enough negative that the resulting table index falls outside the bounds of ff_aac_pow2sf_tab, causing an out-of-bounds array read (verified by an OSS-Fuzz crash on the AAC_LATM decoder).
findings.suggestion: Clamp the updated sfo value to a valid lower bound before storing it, e.g. use FFMAX to ensure sfo never drops below the minimum value accepted by the pow2sf_tab / dequantization logic (the fix commit uses -200 as the lower bound).
findings.title: Unbounded noise_offset accumulation into sce->sfo causes out-of-bounds table read

The bitstream-controlled noise.offset field combined with repeated/attacker-influenced sfo values allowed the stored offset to become large enough to index outside the pow2sf lookup table.

agent_reasoning: Merged diff composed mechanically by cherry-picking fix 23592f942db9 on top of intro 095f8038fa91 via git's 3-way merge. Vulnerability (IntegerOverflow): The yuv2rgba64_full_1_c_template() function (and the closely related yuv2rgba64_1_c_template()) in libswscale/output.c computes chroma (U/V) intermediate values for the bilinear chroma interpolation path using a weighted sum of two 32-bit chroma sample buffers multiplied by interpolation weights (uvalpha/uvalpha1), followed by subtracting a bias constant and right-shifting. This intermediate value is stored in a plain signed `int`. For certain crafted/adversarial input pixel data (as found by OSS-Fuzz's SWS_fuzzer), the multiply-accumulate expression can overflow the range representable by a 32-bit signed int, which is undefined behavior in C and is detected by UndefinedBehaviorSanitizer. Root cause: When the bilinear chroma interpolation code path was rewritten to use a true weighted average (`ubuf0[i]*uvalpha1 + ubuf1[i]*uvalpha`) instead of the previous simple sum/average (`ubuf0[i] + ubuf1[i]`), the resulting intermediate value's magnitude range increased, but the variable holding it was left declared as a plain signed `int` instead of the project's overflow-tolerant `SUINT` (unsigned int) type that other intermediate values (like Y) in the same function already use to safely allow wraparound instead of hitting signed-overflow UB.
commit_message:
swscale/output: fix bilinear yuv2rgb chroma interpolation

These functions were divided into two special cases; one assuming that
uvalpha == 0, and the other assuming that uvalpha == 2048. This worked fine
for simple 2x chroma upscaling but broke for e.g. yuv410p, non-centered chroma,
or other special cases that involved non-aligned chroma filters.

Fix it by instead dividing this check into two cases, a uvalpha==0 fast path
and a uvalpha>0 general path. Instead of (A+B)/2 the general path now multiplies
in the true uvalpha weight.

I tried preserving the old fast path for the case of uvalpha == 2048, but this
was significantly slower in practise versus having just one general path.
However, we still need a uvalpha == 0 path for the unscaled case.

Fixes: ticket #5083
Signed-off-by: Niklas Haas <git@haasn.dev>

findings.message: In the uvalpha>0 (bilinear chroma interpolation) branch of yuv2rgba64_full_1_c_template(), the U and V chroma values are computed as a weighted sum of two 32-bit chroma samples multiplied by interpolation weights, then a bias is subtracted, and the result is shifted right: `int U = (ubuf0[i] * uvalpha1 + ubuf1[i] * uvalpha - (128 << 23)) >> 14;` (and analogous line for V). U and V are declared as plain signed `int`. Because ubuf0[i]/ubuf1[i] can be large 32-bit intermediate chroma values and uvalpha/uvalpha1 sum to 4096, the multiply-add can exceed INT_MAX/underflow INT_MIN, producing signed integer overflow, which is undefined behavior in C and was flagged by UBSan/OSS-Fuzz (`signed integer overflow: -293650 * 16525 cannot be represented in type 'int'`). This same pattern was introduced in this commit for both the 64-bit full (yuv2rgba64_full_1_c_template) and non-full (yuv2rgba64_1_c_template) variants when the code was changed from a simple average of two chroma samples to a true weighted multiply based on uvalpha.
findings.suggestion: Declare U and V using the project's SUINT macro (which resolves to `unsigned int` in normal builds and `int` only under the CHECKED/UBSan debug configuration) instead of a bare `int`, so that the arithmetic wraps deterministically under modular unsigned arithmetic rather than invoking signed-overflow undefined behavior. This matches the pattern already used for Y in the same function and was the actual fix applied upstream.
findings.suggestion_code:
SUINT U = (ubuf0[i] * uvalpha1 + ubuf1[i] * uvalpha - (128 << 23)) >> 14;
SUINT V = (vbuf0[i] * uvalpha1 + vbuf1[i] * uvalpha - (128 << 23)) >> 14;
findings.title: Signed integer overflow computing chroma weighted sum in yuv2rgba64_full_1_c_template()
